# Funding sources for early-stage IGH and skin-colour measurement research (external report, 2026-11-27)

> **Origin:** report from an outside AI deep-research tool, written from a prompt the project coordinator gave Ben; pasted by Ben into the project chat on 2026-11-28 at 00:57 UTC. The report itself says it was checked on 2026-11-27.
> **Status: unverified, planning only, not legal advice.** Nothing here is evidence for the ledger. Saved verbatim below the line; only this header and the spot-check appendix at the end were added. See "Spot-check" at the bottom for which claims were confirmed against official pages on 2026-11-28.

---

Early-stage research on age- and UV-induced hypopigmentation (idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, photoaged hypopigmentation, melanocyte senescence) and validated skin-colour measurement spans three distinct funding tracks: cutaneous biology (NIAMS, dermatology and pigment foundations), cellular ageing/senescence (NIA, longevity micro-funders), and optical/imaging instrumentation (NIBIB, NSF/NIH SBIR/STTR, cosmetic R&D).

All programme details below were verified on November 27, 2026. Where official programme pages do not publish a specific figure or requirement, the field is marked not found.

1. NIH Institutes and Mechanisms

Three NIH Institutes map directly to this topic:

⚬ NIAMS (National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases): Cutaneous biology, melanocyte dysfunction, photoageing, and pigmentary disorders.
⚬ NIA (National Institute on Aging): Cellular senescence, photoageing biology, and non-invasive biomarkers of ageing.
⚬ NIBIB (National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering): Optical hardware, spectroscopy, colorimetry, and validated imaging/measurement methods.

NIH Small Research Grant Program (Parent R03, Clinical Trial Not Allowed — PA-25-302)

⚬ Institute Fit: NIA and NIBIB participate (supports methodology/technology development, pilot studies, and secondary data analysis). NIAMS does not participate in PA-25-302.
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Higher education institutions, nonprofits, small businesses, and other for-profit organizations with active SAM/eRA Commons registrations. Any individual with the necessary skills, knowledge, and institutional resources may serve as Principal Investigator (PI).
⚬ Typical Award Size: Direct costs of "up to $50,000 per year" for up to 2 years (up to $100,000 total direct costs; non-renewable).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Standard NIH cycles — February 16, June 16, October 16 annually (NOFO expires January 8, 2028).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: "No preliminary data are required but may be included if available."
⚬ Official URL: PA-25-302 and NIH R03 Overview (Checked: November 27, 2026)

NIH Exploratory/Developmental Research Project Grant (Parent R21 — PA-25-304 / PA-25-306)

⚬ Institute Fit: NIAMS (rejoined August 12, 2025 via NOT-AR-25-019 and NOT-AR-25-020), NIA, and NIBIB (PA-25-304, Clinical Trial Not Allowed). Use PA-25-306 if the skin-colour measurement validation constitutes a clinical trial under NIH's definition. (Note: NIBIB's dedicated Trailblazer R21, PA-25-169, expired May 8, 2026; a current reissue was not found.)
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Higher education institutions, nonprofits, small businesses, and other for-profit organizations; PI must have the required expertise and institutional environment.
⚬ Typical Award Size: "Up to $275,000 total in direct costs for the two years, with no more than $200,000 in any year" (non-renewable).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Standard NIH cycles — February 16, June 16, October 16 annually (expires January 8, 2028).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: "Preliminary data are not required for R21 applications; however, they may be included if available." Reviewers expect strong scientific rationale and high-risk/high-reward feasibility.
⚬ Official URL: PA-25-304, PA-25-306, and NIH R21 Overview (Checked: November 27, 2026)

NIH SBIR (Parent R43/R44 — PA-27-100) and STTR (Parent R41/R42 — PA-27-102)

⚬ Institute Fit: NIAMS, NIA, and NIBIB all fund commercializable diagnostic/measurement instruments, imaging software, and therapeutic discovery platforms.
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Applicant must be a U.S. for-profit small business (fewer than 500 employees, greater than 50% owned by U.S. citizens or permanent residents, work performed in the U.S.).
  ⚬ SBIR: No university affiliation required. PI must be primarily employed (greater than 50%) by the small business; up to 33% of Phase I work may be outsourced.
  ⚬ STTR: Requires a formal partnership with a U.S. nonprofit research institution (minimum 40% of work by the small business, minimum 30% by the research institution). PI may be employed by either entity.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Standard NIH budget guidelines (total costs, subject to institute caps): Phase I "$335,937" (6 months to 2 years); Phase II "$2,239,578" (1 to 3 years).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Three standard due dates per year — January 5, April 5, September 5 (PA-27-100 and PA-27-102 expire April 6, 2027).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Official NIH SEED guidance states "Pilot data not required for Phase I application" (Phase I establishes feasibility). Proof-of-concept data are mandatory for Phase II and Direct-to-Phase II.
⚬ Official URL: NIH SEED Program Basics and NIH SBIR/STTR Opportunities (Checked: November 27, 2026)

2. Dermatology Foundations and Societies

Dermatology Foundation (DF) — Research Grants & Career Development Awards

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Research must be conducted in the U.S. under the sponsorship of an ACGME-approved dermatology department or division. Applicants must be early-career investigators: MD, MD/PhD, or DO no more than 12 years past terminal degree, or PhD no more than 8 years past terminal degree (as of January 1, 2027). Independent non-academic applicants cannot serve as lead PI.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Research Grants: "$25,000" (1 year; cannot pay PI salary, travel, or indirect costs). Career Development Awards (CDAs): "$75,000" annual stipend (renewable for 1 additional year). Fellowships: "$35,000".
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual — October 15 (2026 cycle closed October 15, 2026; funding begins July 1; renewals due January 1, 2027).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found in public web summaries (full instructions are in the CDAFG Applicant Instructions PDF; peer review mirrors NIH scientific merit standards).
⚬ Official URL: DF Research Grants and DF Career Development Awards (Checked: November 27, 2026)

American Skin Association (ASA) — Research Grants & Investigative Scientist Awards

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Active researchers in dermatology (no age limit; preference for investigators without prior funding or in formative/mid-career transition stages). Requires an endorsement letter from a Chair of Dermatology confirming institutional commitment (each Chair may endorse only one Research Grant applicant per area per year) and IRB/IACUC approval before funds disburse.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Disease-area Research Grants: "$15,000" (no salary, travel, tuition, or indirect costs). Investigative Scientist Awards (e.g., Sun Pharma or Calder awards): "$100,000". Medical Student Grants: "$7,000".
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual — 2026 deadline was June 19, 2026 (2027 exact date: not found).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Not explicitly required in the 2-page Research Grant format (calls for title, purpose, materials, methods, and projected results). Specific preliminary data requirement for Investigative Scientist Awards: not found.
⚬ Official URL: ASA For Grant Seekers (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Skin of Color Society (SOCS) — Dermatology Research Award

⚬ Relevance Note: Directly aligned with validated skin-colour measurement across diverse phototypes and hypopigmentation disorders. Crucial hardware caveat: SOCS explicitly prohibits spending grant funds on capital equipment including "camera equipment, sensors, computers, or tablets."
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Active SOCS member holding an MD, DO, or international equivalent at a U.S.-accredited program/organization (dermatology residents, formal dermatology research fellows, or board-certified/eligible dermatologists within 8 years post-training), with a mentor letter of commitment.
⚬ Typical Award Size: "Up to $20,000" (non-renewable; 18-month completion window; excludes salary, indirect costs, IRB fees, and capital equipment). (Note: SOCS also co-sponsors the DF–SOCS Collaborative Mid-Career Research Award at "$100,000 in annual support for up to three years" for dermatology faculty within 12 years of Assistant Professor appointment; deadline December 1 — DF–SOCS Guidelines PDF.)
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual — opens August 1, closes mid-October (e.g., October 13/15; exact 2027 date: not found).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found (application requests objective, rationale, methods, significance, and optional reprints).
⚬ Official URL: SOCS Dermatology Research Award and SOCS Application Details (Checked: November 27, 2026)

LEO Foundation — Research Grants (International & European Calls)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Independent academic and nonprofit dermatology researchers worldwide. Explicitly excludes research projects involving commercial companies and projects focused on skin cancer (note: benign photoaged hypopigmentation and skin-measurement methods are in scope, provided no commercial company is involved).
⚬ Typical Award Size: Cap for the 2026 International Research Grants call not found in public summaries (for reference, LEO Foundation's Visiting Researchers grant is up to "DKK 2 million", and its early-career ISID–LEO Foundation Award is "USD 100,000"). Indirect costs are capped at 5%.
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual international call in autumn (2026 call ran October 1 – November 23, 2026, now closed). New European call opens June 10, 2027 and closes July 30, 2027.
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific threshold not found (governed by the call-specific Application Guide inside the LEOnora portal).
⚬ Official URL: LEO Foundation Research Grants and All LEO Grants & Awards (Checked: November 27, 2026)

(Analyst note on the Society for Investigative Dermatology [SID]: Its official grants portal — sidnet.org/member-center/grants, checked November 27, 2026 — primarily administers travel grants such as "$1,500" collegiality awards, trainee fellowships, and the co-branded ISID–LEO Foundation Award ["USD $100,000"] rather than open early-stage project grants.)

3. Vitiligo and Pigment Research Foundations

Most pigment foundations restrict scope to vitiligo, but proposals focused on validated depigmentation/skin-colour measurement tools or melanocyte survival/senescence pathways can qualify if framed around vitiligo endpoints or broader pigment-cell disorders.

American Skin Association (ASA) — Vitiligo / Pigment Cell Disorders Grants

⚬ Scope Fit: Explicitly covers "vitiligo/pigment cell disorders" (the broadest pigment scope among U.S. dermatology foundations).
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Same as ASA above — active dermatology researcher with Chair of Dermatology endorsement and institutional sponsorship.
⚬ Typical Award Size: ASA Calder Investigative Scientist Award in Vitiligo: "$100,000"; ASA Mulvaney Family Foundation Research Grant in Vitiligo: "$15,000"; Mulvaney Medical Student Grant: "$7,000".
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual — 2026 cycle closed June 19, 2026 (2027 date: not found).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found in public summaries.
⚬ Official URL: ASA For Grant Seekers (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Global Vitiligo Foundation (GVF) — Career Development Award (with Dermatology Foundation)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Administered through the Dermatology Foundation CDA portal; requires U.S. ACGME-approved dermatology department sponsorship and early-career status (MD/DO up to 12 years or PhD up to 8 years post-terminal degree). Must advance vitiligo science or patient care.
⚬ Typical Award Size: "$75,000" (annual stipend; GVF is funding one dedicated vitiligo CDA in 2027).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual — October 15 via the Dermatology Foundation portal.
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found.
⚬ Official URL: GVF Research Grants and DF Career Development Awards (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Vitiligo Research Foundation (VRF) — Research Grants

⚬ Scope Fit: Explicitly supports projects to "experimentally validate the perspective diagnostic methods, tools and treatments in vitiligo" — a direct match for validated skin-colour measurement if applied to vitiligo lesions.
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): PI must hold a "full-time position in academic research lab, hospital or clinical unit"; funding agreement is executed with the administering organization.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Maximum "$50,000 per year" for up to 24 months (up to $100,000 total).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Rolling ("There are no deadlines for Pre-Application submission"); two-stage review starting with an emailed Pre-Application / Letter of Inquiry. (Analyst caveat: VRF's public "Current Grants" page lists awards only through 2021; confirm active funding availability with grants@vrfoundation.org before investing proposal time.)
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Pre-application asks for prior PI contributions and up to 5 key vitiligo publications; diagnostic tool projects must rest on "firm scientific and experimental ground" (exact minimum dataset threshold: not found).
⚬ Official URL: VRF Pre-Application Form and VRF Research Tools & Grants (Checked: November 27, 2026)

(Analyst note on the PanAmerican Society for Pigment Cell Research [PASPCR]: Checked at pas-pcr.org/award-criteria on November 27, 2026 — PASPCR offers trainee/junior-faculty travel awards and recognition awards such as the Medrano Young Investigator Award rather than standalone research project grants [project grant amounts: not found]. It remains a high-value network for recruiting an academic pigment-biology PI partner.)

4. Industry and Cosmetic-Company Research Programmes

Major cosmetic and dermatology companies rarely publish fixed open-call grant amounts for non-clinical basic science; instead, they fund through clinician-focused investigator grants or open-innovation R&D partnering portals.

La Roche-Posay (L'Oréal Dermatological Beauty) — Young Investigator Grant (USA)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): U.S.-based licensed dermatologists (MD/DO) within 5 years post-residency, dermatology residents, or post-residency fellows authorized by their university/institution. Strictly clinical research (animal testing prohibited).
⚬ Typical Award Size: Total award pool of "up to $50,000" across recipients for the 2026/2027 cycle (individual amounts vary by proposal budget and merit; restricted to primary research expenses).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Annual — 2026 cycle is closed (winners notified February 2027); 2027 cycle opens January 4, 2027 (exact 2027 closing date: not found).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Not explicitly mandated (requires an up-to-8-page clinical research plan, itemized budget, CV, and mentor or Chief of Dermatology support letter).
⚬ Official URL: La Roche-Posay Grant Proposal and Terms & Conditions (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Galderma — Investigator-Initiated Studies (IIS)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): "Academic and community based clinician-scientists" conducting independent clinical research aligned with Galderma's focus areas (Aesthetics, Consumer Skincare/Cetaphil, Prescription Dermatology). Galderma does not act as the regulatory study sponsor.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Not found (tailored to approved study budget; monetary funding, in-kind product, or both).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Rolling (unsolicited proposals accepted continuously via the Medical Grants Portal).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found (reviewed on scientific merit, investigator qualifications, budget, strategic alignment, and site feasibility).
⚬ Official URL: Galderma Medical Community Support and Galderma Medical Grants Portal (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Beiersdorf — Open Innovation ("Collaborate to Innovate")

⚬ Scope Fit: Explicitly invites external partners on skin care, UV filters, and longevity/ageing skin science (Beiersdorf also operates a €100M corporate venture capital fund targeting startups in longevity science and actives discovery, though that is equity investment rather than grant funding).
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Open globally to "research institutes, universities, start-ups, independent scientists and suppliers" — one of the few corporate R&D entry points that explicitly welcomes independent scientists without a university affiliation.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Not found (structured as negotiated sponsored research, co-development, or licensing contracts rather than fixed grants).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Rolling (proactive ideas and open innovation challenges accepted year-round).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific threshold not found (proactive submissions typically benefit from a working prototype, assay data, or patent/technical dossier).
⚬ Official URL: Beiersdorf Open Innovation (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Halo Science — Corporate Open Innovation RFPs (e.g., Henkel, Kimberly-Clark, Consumer Skin/Personal Care)

⚬ Scope Fit: Industry partnering marketplace where consumer-goods and personal-care R&D divisions post active technical briefs (including skin science, optical/surface measurement, and barrier/ageing research) for proof-of-concept testing, sponsored research, or fee-for-service pilots.
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Universities, startups, and independent R&D labs/innovators (exact eligibility varies per corporate brief).
⚬ Typical Award Size: Not found (set per corporate RFP / negotiated contract).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Rolling / per-RFP depending on active sponsor briefs.
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Varies by RFP (typically expects demonstrated technical capability or prototype; uniform threshold: not found).
⚬ Official URL: Halo Science – Kimberly-Clark Skin Health RFPs and Halo – Henkel R&D Case Study (Checked: November 27, 2026)

5. Prizes and Seed Grants Open Without a University Affiliation

NSF SBIR / STTR — America's Seed Fund (Solicitation NSF 26-510)

⚬ Scope Fit: Prime non-dilutive vehicle for an independent engineer building a validated skin-colour measurement device, optical sensor, or computer-vision colorimetry pipeline.
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): U.S. for-profit small business (fewer than 500 employees; at least 50% owned by U.S. citizens or permanent residents; not majority-owned by VC/PE/hedge funds). PI must be legally employed at least 20 hours/week by the company and commit at least 1 calendar month per 6 months. NSF explicitly notes: "The PI doesn't need any advanced degrees." No university affiliation is required for SBIR.
⚬ Typical Award Size: Phase I: "up to $305,000" (6–18 months); Phase II: "up to $1,250,000" (24 months); Fast-Track: "up to $1,555,555" (requires prior NSF research lineage).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Mandatory Project Pitch is rolling (decision in 1–2 months). Invited full-proposal deadlines: March 4, 2027 (first Thursday in March), first Wednesday in July, and first Wednesday in November annually.
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Minimal for Phase I — specifically funds R&D on "unproven, high-impact innovations" to prove technical feasibility and reduce technical risk. Phase II requires Phase I feasibility results.
⚬ Official URL: NSF 26-510 Solicitation and NSF Seed Fund Get Started (Checked: November 27, 2026)

NIH SBIR Phase I (Parent R43 — PA-27-100)

⚬ (Full details listed in Section 1.) Requires forming a U.S. small business (LLC or C-Corp), not a university affiliation. Award guideline: "$335,937"; deadlines January 5, April 5, September 5; pilot data not required for Phase I.
⚬ Official URL: NIH SEED Program Basics (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Emergent Ventures (Mercatus Center at George Mason University)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Any individual "at least 13 years old" worldwide — no university affiliation, degree, or registered company required. (Important rule: Emergent Ventures tests and rejects AI-written applications beyond basic proofreading.)
⚬ Typical Award Size: Official dollar range not found on the Mercatus landing page (awards are flexible, low-overhead grants/fellowships sized to the project).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Rolling (limit one application per applicant and project).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found (evaluates high-leverage "zero to one" ideas and founder execution rather than formal lab data).
⚬ Official URL: Emergent Ventures (Checked: November 27, 2026)

Longevity Impetus Grants (Norn Group)

⚬ Scope Fit: Directly relevant to melanocyte senescence, photoageing biology, and longitudinal skin-ageing biomarker datasets.
⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Listed as "Any" target group with no U.S. citizenship requirement (explicitly funds researchers new to ageing biology; exact disbursement rules for unaffiliated individuals vs. 501(c)(3)/academic hosts per round: not found on official site).
⚬ Typical Award Size: Official per-grant cap not found on the primary website (launch announcement cited a "$26M" total pool; third-party grant trackers report individual grants up to "$500,000" depending on the round).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Variable / round-specific (designed for rapid ~3-week decisions when a call is open; current open/close dates: not found on official site).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: Specific requirement not found (explicitly aims to test bold, early-stage hypotheses that lack sufficient data for NIA R01 funding).
⚬ Official URL: impetusgrants.org (referenced via American Aging Association Funding Directory, Checked: November 27, 2026)

Experiment.com (Science Crowdfunding & Experiment Foundation)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Open to independent researchers, citizen scientists, students, and academics (staff review every proposal; payouts limited to eligible countries including the U.S.).
⚬ Typical Award Size: Variable, all-or-nothing crowdfunding; company-reported average funded project is "$3,372" (8% platform fee plus payment processing if successful; zero university indirect overhead).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Rolling (campaigns typically run 30–45 days once approved).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: None required (empirical analyses show prior publications do not drive funding success; a clear protocol, transparent budget, and public communication do).
⚬ Official URL: Experiment.com (metrics cross-verified via September 2026 audit at healthcarediscovery.ai/companies/experiment, Checked: November 27, 2026)

The Awesome Foundation (Microgrants)

⚬ Eligibility (Lead Applicant): Anyone — individuals, teams, nonprofits, or companies worldwide (chapter-specific scope; no university affiliation required). Best suited for open-source skin-colour calibration targets, open datasets, or community health/education tools rather than general startup overhead.
⚬ Typical Award Size: "$1,000" (no-strings-attached microgrant).
⚬ Deadlines / Cycle: Monthly (or bi-monthly, depending on the chapter).
⚬ Preliminary Data Expected: None — requires a concise, concrete plan showing how $1,000 delivers immediate progress.
⚬ Official URL: The Awesome Foundation (Checked: November 27, 2026)

6. How an Independent Engineer Partners with an Academic or Clinical Lead

Because dermatology foundations (DF, ASA, SOCS, GVF, LEO) and clinical industry grants (LRP, Galderma) restrict lead-applicant status to university faculty or licensed dermatologists—and because human skin-colour validation requires IRB approval and access to phenotyped patient cohorts—independent engineers typically use one of five standard partnership structures:

1. Engineer's Small Business as Prime Applicant, University as Subawardee (NIH/NSF STTR or SBIR):
  ⚬ Form a U.S. LLC or C-Corp (takes days; SAM/UEI registration takes 2–4 weeks).
  ⚬ In STTR, the university dermatology lab is a mandatory formal partner (handling at least 30% of the work: IRB protocol, patient recruitment across Fitzpatrick phototypes, dermatology grading, or melanocyte senescence biopsies), while the engineer's company performs at least 40% (optics, calibration hardware, colorimetry algorithms). Either party can be PI, and the money flows to the small business.
  ⚬ In SBIR, the engineer is PI (employed greater than 50% by the small business) and brings the dermatologist in either as a subawardee (up to 33% of Phase I) or as a paid individual consultant (often faster and free of university indirect-cost overhead, provided the professor's university allows external consulting).
2. Academic/Clinical PI as Prime Applicant, Engineer as Fee-for-Service Vendor or Consultant (Foundations, NIH R03/R21, Industry IIS):
  ⚬ The dermatologist or pigment biologist submits as lead PI through their university.
  ⚬ The engineer is budgeted as an independent consultant (fixed hourly/milestone fee for algorithm validation or optical engineering) or commercial vendor (delivering custom calibration hardware or software).
  ⚬ Watch the fine print: Check funder exclusions before budgeting. For example, LEO Foundation bans projects involving commercial companies, and SOCS bans purchasing cameras, sensors, or computers.
3. Academic Prime + Small-Business Subaward / Multiple PI (MPI) on NIH R03/R21:
  ⚬ For NIH R03 or R21 proposals led by a university, the engineer's LLC can receive a formal subaward (listing the engineer as Key Personnel, Co-Investigator, or Co-PI under a Multiple PI Leadership Plan). This requires the engineer's entity to hold a SAM UEI and basic federal financial-compliance controls.
4. Unsalaried Visiting Scientist / Adjunct / Affiliate Appointment:
  ⚬ Many academic dermatology departments grant Visiting Scholar, Research Affiliate, or Adjunct appointments to collaborating engineers. This lets you be named directly on the university's IRB protocol, access dermatology clinic imaging rooms and spectrophotometer cores, and co-author validation papers without formal subcontracts.
5. Pre-Submission Agreements That Prevent Deadlocks:
  ⚬ IRB Ownership: Let the university or clinical site act as the IRB of record for human-subject skin imaging; commercial IRBs cost thousands of dollars out of pocket and still require a clinical site.
  ⚬ IP & Data Allocation: Before submission, sign a brief Memorandum of Understanding (or the legally required STTR IP Allocation Agreement prior to award) separating background IP (your existing sensor/algorithm design) from foreground IP (jointly validated clinical endpoints or datasets), plus a Data Use Agreement (DUA) allowing you to retain de-identified spectral/colour calibration data.

## What this means for Ben (this project's judgment, 2026-11-28; covers this report and the ethics report)

This is judgment, not legal or funding advice. It uses only the claims marked FOUND above and in `ethics-regulatory-2026-11-27.md`.

**Ethics, before photographing anyone other than yourself**

1. Get a written determination from an independent IRB before recruiting anyone. Without federal money or a university, the Common Rule may not legally apply (45 CFR 46.101(a)), but ICMJE journals expect approval from "an independent ... review body", so skipping it would make the data unpublishable. Solutions IRB's posted fees are $925 for a non-human-subject determination, $1,200 for an exempt review and $2,100 for a social/behavioral expedited review, plus extras such as revision rounds at $350 to $550. Budget about $2,000 to $2,500. The likely route is expedited category 6, image recordings made for research.
2. Write the IRB package before paying: the protocol (the open study proposal, PR 6, is a start), a consent form with a separate yes or no for publishing images, and a data plan (coded file names, metadata stripped, no phone cloud sync, the name key kept apart from the images). The repository's no-patient-images rule already fits this.
3. Keep biopsies out of the first protocol. A research-only biopsy does not fit the noninvasive expedited category, so it would need full-board review and a dermatologist. Add it later as an amendment, ideally under a clinical partner's IRB. The state law where you live was not checked; tell me the state if you want that looked at.

**Funding, most realistic routes**

1. **Microgrants and crowdfunding, now.** The Awesome Foundation gives "$1,000 grants every month" to anyone, and Experiment.com is all-or-nothing with an 8% fee plus 3 to 5% payment processing. Either fits the camera kit and colour card scale. You need a short public project description and budget first. Posting one is public, so it needs your yes under the project's own rules.
2. **NSF SBIR Phase I (NSF 26-510), up to $305,000 for 6 to 18 months.** This fits a validated skin-colour measurement tool, not a treatment. The PI "doesn't need any advanced degrees" but must be employed at least 20 hours a week by the company. You would first set up a US small business (LLC or corporation), a SAM.gov/UEI registration (from the report, not checked), and an accepted Project Pitch. The next full-proposal deadline is March 4, 2027.
3. **A partnered NIH grant (R21, up to $275,000 direct over two years, NIAMS participates) or NIH STTR.** You would first need a university dermatologist or pigment researcher willing to be lead or partner. Their IRB would then likely become the reviewing IRB, which would replace step 1 above. Of the three routes, this is the only one that can lead to biopsies and the cell-level questions in Module 5.
